title: Every word has a tune
hook: the Tanakh is chanted with ancient musical notes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orchard of four readings: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Your line was plain meaning first. Did you read a message for what it actually said? Today, the last day of our time in the Writings, and a way of reading you hear with your ears. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

Tiny marks, above and below the letters. Open a printed Hebrew Bible and look closely: besides the letters, and the vowel dots, there's a third layer of small signs scattered across the verses. A little wedge here, a curl there, a dot beside a line. Those marks are the trope, in Hebrew te'amim. They tell a reader how to chant. The Torah scroll itself has no vowels and no marks at all, so the reader learns them beforehand. In the synagogue, the Torah is chanted, word by word, each word carrying its own short phrase of melody, and the marks say which phrase. So this whole library we've been reading, the Torah, the Prophets, the Writings, carries its music on the page.
screen: `A THIRD LAYER OF MARKS.` → `TROPE: TE'AMIM.` → `THE TEXT IS SUNG.`

segments.voice: The trope does two jobs at once. The first is music: each mark is a little melody, and a verse becomes a chain of them. The second is sense. The same marks work like punctuation. Some say pause here, strongly. Some say keep going, these words belong together. So the tune is also a guide to meaning: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Take the first verse of the Torah, in the King James words: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In the Hebrew, the main pause mark falls after God created, and the chant rests there, before the heaven and the earth. Read it with the tune, and the verse has a shape. The Hebrew word ta'am, the singular of te'amim, can mean taste, and also sense or reason. And here's a link back to the water gate. When the book of Nehemiah says the Levites read distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading, the Talmud reads part of that verse as the te'amim themselves. On that reading, understanding the text and hearing where it divides go together. One more thing. Tradition has more than one melody for the same marks, and some books, like Esther on Purim and Lamentations on the ninth of Av, have tunes of their own. Same marks, many voices. Lately we've walked through the Writings: wisdom, song, lament, Esther, Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, Chronicles. Today, the marks that carry all of it as song.
screen: `MARKS THAT ARE MUSIC.` · `MARKS THAT ARE PUNCTUATION.` · then, large: `WHERE IT BREATHES, IT DIVIDES.` · then: `SAME MARKS, MANY MELODIES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to listen to one chanted verse. Sit, and let the room go quiet. If you've ever heard Torah chanted, at a synagogue, a bar or bat mitzvah, a recording, let a few notes of it come back now. If you haven't, take the first verse of Genesis and say it slowly to yourself, pausing after God created, then going on: the heaven and the earth. Listen to where the pause falls. Say it again, and let your voice rise and fall a little, any way that feels natural. After the bell, if you'd like, find one recording of a chanted verse and listen with your eyes closed. The bell holds the time.
Trope. The small marks in the Hebrew text that give each word its melody and show where the verse pauses: in Hebrew, te'amim. Today's word.
Your line: every word has a tune. Today, read one sentence that matters to you out loud, slowly, and listen for where it wants to pause. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: In synagogue, a reader chants the Torah and haftarah portions from the text using the te'amim, and young people preparing for a bar or bat mitzvah learn the trope to chant their portion.

original.note: Hebrew: te'amim, the trope marks; ta'am can mean taste, and also sense.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Torah is just read aloud.
what it means: small marks in the text give each word a melody, so the Tanakh is chanted, not spoken.
what a scholar hears: the marks are also syntax, dividing each verse by its sense, and the Talmud reads Nehemiah 8:8's understanding as the te'amim.

notes: Index hook says 'ancient musical notes'; the script avoids dating the te'amim and says only that they are marks in the text. Keeper may add dating if a cited source supports it.
Nedarim 37b / Megillah 3a: 'and caused them to understand the reading' read as the pisuk te'amim (some say the masoretic notes). Please confirm the paraphrase and which half of the verse is meant.
Genesis 1:1: main pause (etnachta) on Elohim, after 'God created'. Please confirm.
Claims that different communities use different melodies, and that Esther and Lamentations have their own tunes, are standard but not in the cited texts; confirm.
